Tools · in the spacetime diagram

Behind the timetable

What is calculated, and what is drawn.

Times are in seconds and distances in light-seconds (ls), so light moves 1 ls per second and every light ray in the diagram climbs at 45°. Speeds are fractions of the speed of light, c.

Every position, time and clock reading comes from the Lorentz transformation between the platform frame and the frame you ride with:

t′ = γ (t − v x), x′ = γ (x − v t), γ = 1/√(1 − v²)

Clocks and simultaneity

Each train’s clocks are synchronised in that train’s own frame, by Einstein’s convention (light signals take equal times both ways). Seen from another frame, a moving train’s clocks run slow by γ and are out of step along its length: the clock at the front lags the one at the back by v L₀, where L₀ is the train’s own length. That is why the same pair of events can be simultaneous for one train and not for another.

Lengths

A moving train is shorter by γ, because measuring its length means marking both ends at the same moment, and “the same moment” differs between frames. Nothing is squeezed: in its own frame the train is always L₀ long.

Invariants

The interval s² = Δt² − Δx² between two events is the same in every frame. The curves t² − x² = constant are drawn in the diagram; they do not move when you change trains, while everything else slides along them.

The twins

The traveller turns round instantly. Riding with it, its “now” line swings at the turn, and the home clock’s reading on that line jumps forward: that is where the extra years of the stay-at-home twin are found.

Keys

Space pause · R restart · 1–7 routes · F next frame.

Drawn for clarity: the height of the trains, the clock faces and the speed of play. Trains are rigid and move in straight lines (the traveller’s turn is instant), and nothing here includes gravity or the travel time of light to your eye: what is shown is what each frame measures, not what a camera would see.
